To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we found defects in the cytoplamic preassembly of axonemel dynein arms to cause morphological abnormalities in sperm cells leading male infertility.

we identified a complete loss of outer dynein arms and inner dynein arms as well as a reduced length of sperm flagella of PCD patients with defects in the cytoplamic assembly of axonemes, which is relevant for their fertility status.
mutations in genes encoding factors involved in the cytoplamic assembly of axoneme dynein arms also affect sperm flagella and cause male infertility.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cytoplasmatic assembly of axonemeal dynein arm in spermatozoa and its clinical relevance on fertility in PCD patients.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms that underlie the pathogenesis of human male infertility.
the molecular mechanisms of ciliary motility and the clinical consequences of ciliary dysfunction in sperm cells and respiratory cilia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
sperm flagella are not just miniature versions of respiratory cilia, but have distinct features in composition and assembly.
the cytoplasmatic assembly of dynein axonemes is essential for sperm motility and thus fertility in humans.
sperm flagella and motility are impaired in PCD patients, but not completely abolished.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
axonemally assembled dynein arms play a critical role in sperm function and flagellar structure, thus male fertility.
the process of dynein pre-assembly is also critical for the generation of functional sperm, and the loss of dynein assembly in sperm is associated with male infertility.
the cytoplasmatic dynein pre-assembly process is essential for the formation of functional cilia and flagella.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sperm from PCD patients are not only structurally abnormal, but also functionally impaired.
axonemally localized dynein arms can be lost or reduced in PCD- affected males, which is relevant for the diagnosis of PCD.
the axonemal assembly of dynein prearms is critical for the generation of sperm flagella and thus male fertility.
